articles.title: Pope Leo XIV on AI
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.
I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.
First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined .” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”
Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”
Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”
Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”
I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014 , with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.
Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.
Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said , adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”
I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.
Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.
Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk , but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.
Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

articles.title: Feeding more than 100 a day with Community Lunch on Capitol Hill
articles.author: CHS
paras: By Brenna Gauchat On a Monday morning, you can stop by Community Lunch on Capitol Hill’s breakfast service for a hot coffee and pastry, then return later for lunch and dinner leftovers. Operating out of All Pilgrims Christian Church , the Capitol Hill-based nonprofit is a non-religious meal service dedicated to serving free, high-quality food every weekday to over 100 guests daily. According to Paul Getzel , the nonprofit’s executive director, the program is on track to serve 120,000 meals this year, including 1,000 plates for Thanksgiving and December holidays. As of August, meal distribution is up 40% year-over-year — a trend Getzel expects to continue.

Getzel attributes this growth to the program’s “barrierless” model, which sets Community Lunch apart from other meal services. Because guests may take unlimited food, the count of meals distributed often outnumbers individuals served, as guests frequently share extra plates with others or save them for later. “What [the meals distributed count] indicates to me is that a lot of people are still representing other people that are outside,” Getzel said about stepping back when someone asks for multiple meals. “Sometimes, when I go out to sort of clean up around the church here, I see folks bringing food to their friends who didn’t come in. They’re just out there for a lot of reasons.” Guests are never asked for identification or names, ensuring access regardless of circumstances.

With many regular guests, staff and volunteers naturally build relationships and rapport over time. “I see some folks that I know that are unhoused, that every day, every minute, every night are living in survival circumstances,” Getzel said, emphasizing the focus on immediate essentials—food, water, clothing, and health services—rather than long-term systemic issues. “What we provide is, at least, some safety and some service and deference. And hopefully some comfort for them. An hour and a half a day for lunch, a little bit longer on the holidays.”

Getzel noted that building neighborhood trust through reliable food access also opens doors for external referrals. “I think one thing that has always really inspired me is when you connect with somebody around their basic needs or on food,” Getzel said. “It’s apt to take a referral to another service, just because you have built that trust with people.”

Beyond meals, Community Lunch distributes clothing and health items such as Naloxone and Plan B. The program also partners with Seattle King County Public Health’s Street Medicine team to provide mobile medical care on site, enabling staff to connect guests needing medical attention directly with trusted providers.

“That warm handoff is really, really helpful with [referrals to external care],” Getzel said. “Based on that relationship, they’re willing to accept care.” Looking ahead, the nonprofit is exploring expansions into low-cost veterinary care and legal or immigration advocacy with groups like Northwest Immigrant Rights Project . “I think one thing that we’re really trying to do this year is be responsive to community need,” Getzel said.

Getzel brings over 25 years of local nonprofit experience to Community Lunch, having previously spent nearly 18 years at Lifelong, including work with its Chicken Soup Brigade food and nutrition program. Now focusing on funding, volunteer recruitment, and holiday prep, Getzel ensures Community Lunch remains open during holidays when other services close. “Need doesn’t stop just because it’s the holidays,” Getzel said. “Assuming that the weather is a little bit nasty by then, we want to make sure, for the holidays, people could get out of the weather at least for a little while.”

While partially funded by city grants, the organization relies primarily on donations to cover expenses. Working with partners like Food Lifeline, the kitchen prepares high-quality holiday meals and requests community support through food and monetary contributions. “We really try to provide an experience where we’re deferring to our guests and we’re serving them because a lot of these folks just don’t experience that ever,” Getzel said. “We don’t want to compromise because we don’t have something for free.”

Supported by six staff members and about 100 weekly volunteers, the program needs consistent volunteer help during holiday meal prep. While Thanksgiving Day sees an influx of volunteers, help is especially needed in the days leading up to the holidays for food preparation. Getzel encourages community members to volunteer with friends and family during the season. “We want everybody,” Getzel said. “We really want to have diversity in every sense of the word, including income and neighborhood you live in, age, everything.”
The lunches also bring together people who want to help. CHS reported here on Community Lunch volunteers who are hoping to inspire the creation of a new “day shelter” facility on Capitol Hill.

At its core, Community Lunch prides itself on offering meals, companionship, shelter, and dignity to the neighborhood. “I just urge for people to not lose their compassion for everybody,” Getzel said. “When we shut ourselves down and dismiss somebody and dehumanize somebody, that’s not going to be a solution. That person’s not going anywhere, and they’re just going to suffer more.”
For more information on how to help, visit communitylunch.org .

articles.title: Sunday Video: How Does Philadelphia Even Exist
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Shortly after his visit to Seattle (where he attending a talk co-hosted by with The Urbanist), Ray Delahanty headed to the East Coast and did a similar event in Philadelphia. Ray had a lot to say about Philly's walkability and other positive aspects that often fly under the radar, sandwiched as the city is between New York City and Washington D.C., which have higher profiles nationally and internationally.

Delahanty declared Philadelphia might have the most walkable city core in the whole United States, which stems in large part from the thoughtful urban plan William Penn made for the city as he founded it in 1682, with plenty of narrow streets friendly to pedestrians.

"These streets are really a microcosm of what I'm thinking about when I think about walkability," Delahanty said. "It's not just about the physical act of walking. It's how a street handles motor vehicles. It's whether the streetscape is visually interesting. It's whether you feel secure. It's whether there are a ton of destinations nearby that are worth walking to."
Philadelphia – at least in the center city and South Philly neighborhoods that Ray explored – checked all those boxes. These distinctions puts it among North America's most walkable cities.

It's not all roses in the City of Brotherly Love. Philadelphia is also dealing with service cuts on SEPTA, a legacy metro system which has an impressive network of rapid transit lines across the region. As Delahanty highlighted, those cuts mean frequencies have decreased, especially on weekends, when even bedrock routes are now seeing mediocre 10-minute headways – not really in line with a top-tier transit city, which boasts a population of 1.5 million, amid a metropolitan region of 6.3 million. Hopefully SEPTA can get out of its downward spiral and back on the path of service improvements and growth.

articles.title: Forget maxxing your life. 2027 must be the year we relax – and start minning | Polly Hudson
articles.author: Polly Hudson
paras: Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, minning means doing them less, if at all

Public service announcement: fellow citizens, we have maxxmaxxinged. It has been close for a while, but now we have gone over the edge – reached, and passed, maximum maxxing. The tipping point was a week in which we saw reports of Namemaxxing . If you can’t decide between two baby names, pick them both. Suggestions included blending Maeve and Avery to create Mavery, or Leo and Giovanni to make Leovanni – Futupid. Then Dictionary.com revealed its word of the year and, yes, you guessed it: maxxing. It’s fully exhausting, in every way, but mainly in that -maxx has been fully exhausted. For the good of us all, 2027 has to be the year of minning. (The second “n” is important, otherwise pits may be deluged.)

Maxxing is selfish, desperately try-hard and often futile – surely nobody who ever set out to funmaxx achieved it (see: New Year’s Eve), not even Dua Lipa . Minning is much more noble: it’s about making the world, rather than only yourself, better. Instead of pushing your endeavours to the limit, it means doing them less, if at all.

articles.title: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare
articles.author: Adrian Horton
paras: The maximalist, heart over head adaptation of the romantic tragedy made stars of its leads and became an English teacher’s most trusted weapon for Bard-averse students

Romeo + Juliet is not the most renowned or beloved of Shakespeare’s plays, but it is perhaps the most foundational. The 16th-century tragedy, a story of love-addled teenagers and white-hot resentment, is often an English student’s first introduction to the bard’s oeuvre – more accessible and relatable to teens, with its plaintive lust and histrionic mood swings, than the more austere machinations in, say, Macbeth, Hamlet or Othello. And if Romeo + Juliet is the young person’s entry to Elizabethan English, perhaps no version of it is more worthy of the term “gateway drug” than Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film version, which reimagined Verona’s family feud as a tropical gang war and launched an army of teenage crushes with the faces of Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes.

The maximalist interpretation of Shakespeare’s most lovelorn work, released 30 years ago this week (!), retains Elizabethan verse but announces its divergence from rigid classicism from the jump. Our scene is set in fair Verona beach by a news anchor via TV set, relaying the woe of two star-cross’d lovers before clips of civil strife. Fresh off his breakout success in 1992’s Strictly Ballroom, the Australian director boldly mapped the medieval story on to 90s tabloid fixations – grainy footage of violence in the streets, magazine headlines of capos and criminals, helicopter views of car chases and riots that recalled the media circus around the OJ Simpson chase two years prior. It is a movie that could have only been made in the 90s; Luhrmann’s vision of two warring families as rival gangs, replete with their own economic operations and marked territory, tapped into the era’s preoccupation with gangland as a source of transportive art, from movies to hip-hop, and as a conservative fixation for ideas on intrinsic criminality.

articles.title: Parents, let your kids eat as much candy as they want – less restriction could help reduce the urge to overeat
articles.author:
<name>Bryn Beeder, Assistant Clinical Lecturer in Kinesiology, Nutrition, and Health, Miami University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/bryn-beeder-2260643"/>
paras: Kids and candy are a classic pairing. From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets, to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home another bag of treats. But while these holidays and events may be exciting for kids, they often end with parents dreading what comes next: negotiations around how much candy to consume.

As a registered dietitian and mom of three, I understand the stress that comes with wanting to encourage healthy food choices without removing all the fun of childhood traditions. I also believe the answer to this dilemma may be simpler than the familiar back and forth of “Just one more piece of candy!” and “Haven’t you had enough already?”

Research suggests that by managing the candy inventory less and encouraging more autonomy around sweets, parents can help their kids practice tapping into their hunger and fullness cues , promoting a healthier relationship with food over time.

There is no question that some foods have greater nutritional value than others. A piece of cake – carrot cake included – will never provide the vitamins and minerals of a large garden salad. As a result, people often categorize different foods as “good” or “bad.”

The tendency to place food in two polarizing buckets can affect everything from what foods you purchase at the grocery store to the language you use to describe food. The problem is, “ good” and “bad” are moral concepts . When morality is consistently applied to food, a person’s relationship to food can become complicated. Instead of viewing food as fueling, it can become a measuring stick for whether your food choices are something to feel proud of or guilty about.

When a person’s inner monologue about food is preoccupied with whether it is good or bad for their health or diet plan, food choices can become less about enjoyment and more about their willpower to make the “right” decision at the grocery store and at mealtimes. Any guilt or shame that comes from this evaluation can spill over into what foods are served freely at home and which are restricted.

The idea of food restriction often sounds punishing. For parents and others who take care of children, food restriction often may simply be an attempt to limit sugary foods and introduce more fruits and vegetables.

But for kids, restricting certain foods may lead them to become preoccupied with those foods . They may be nagged by the knowledge that the foods adults often call “bad” are also the ones that are really delicious. What started as a simple candy rule can continue to influence a child’s relationship to food and eating long after the treats are gone.

Parents often approach food restriction in two different ways . In overt food restriction, kids are aware that their parents or guardians are limiting access to specific foods because they can see it or are told specific foods are off limits. In practice, this might mean the kids know candy is in the house but stored out of reach in the kitchen cupboards. Parents or caregivers who practice covert food restriction, on the other hand, may choose to not buy bags of candy at all in order to encourage more balanced food choices.

Research suggests that overt restriction can unintentionally increase kids’ interest in those restricted food items . That preoccupation may mean the child has a more difficult time listening to their fullness cues when presented with those foods. If bags of candy are usually stored out of reach, it may be tempting to eat more than just a few pieces when access is finally granted – and they may completely ignore any signs that their body is full.

Incorporating neutral language about food at mealtimes and encouraging kids to eat according to their own hunger and fullness cues can help them build trust in their bodies and improve family connection at the table. Taking the pressure off finishing all the food on the plate can instead place emphasis on savoring the sensory experience of each bite.

Eating according to internal cues is one part of intuitive eating , which aims to increase a person’s trust in their own body to signal when to start eating and when to stop. Kids can also benefit from this same framework, with some age-appropriate modifications.

The Satter Division of Responsibility in Feeding provides a simple, research-based approach to feeding kids in a way that avoids power struggles between kids and caretakers at the table. Developed by the Ellyn Satter Institute, a nonprofit focused on improving people’s relationship to food, the goal of the framework is to introduce intuitive eating in a kid-friendly way. When providing food through this approach, parents decide when and what food is served, while kids are in charge of deciding what and how much they eat from their plates. The emphasis is on helping kids eat according to their internal cues without pressuring them to eat specific foods.

Candy can be a part of the menu rotation in this feeding framework. Repeatedly exposing kids to a variety of foods, including sugary treats outside of special holidays or events, means no food becomes emphasized for being better or worse than another food – it is all simply food .

This approach can shift the conversation to how different foods affect their bodies in different ways: Some food – like candy – makes them run super fast, some foods grow their muscles, while other foods keep their eyes strong.

Regularly using neutral language to describe food and exposing kids to a variety of foods helps reduce the power that sugary treats have over their appetites. This doesn’t mean birthday cake, doughnuts and candy will no longer taste delicious. It simply means children can rest assured they will see their favorite treats again without the added urge to overconsume them.
If you’re interested in exploring how intuitive eating principles could change your child’s or your own relationship with food, here are a few practices you can try at home:

Involve children in menu planning and grocery shopping . Let your kids pick a treat to add to a few meals each week, and serve the treat with the rest of the food on the menu for that day. Presenting all food items at the same time on the plate – versus saving a dessert or treat for after the meal – visually reminds everyone that food does not have to be earned. Rather, each food nourishes their bodies in different ways.

Avoid commenting on what your kids eat . It can be tempting to praise a child when they choose to take a bite of the broccoli you’ve been encouraging for weeks. Praising kids for eating certain foods versus others can create a food hierarchy , leading them to think about food as a way to earn a reward instead of fueling their body.

Challenge your own relationship with food . Do you eat when you are hungry and stop when you are full? Do you restrict your own food cravings as a punishment, or do you struggle to control yourself when eating a treat you love? Kids are always watching, and your own food behaviors often speak louder than words.

Consider letting your kids indulge for a day . In my own family, I don’t limit how much candy my three kids eat on Halloween night. I won’t lie – they usually eat quite a bit. When they mention a stomachache afterward, we talk about how eating a lot of candy can make their bodies feel – without adding judgment. Their interest typically fades over the next few days while we continue to offer a piece of two with meals. Eventually the extras become props for elaborate trick-or-treat pretend play.
One day or evening of holiday eating does not define their health , but fun memories with friends and families can last a lifetime. So let them eat … candy!

articles.title: Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer , an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday , saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.
In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”
The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.
“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.
“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.
He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.
Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.
Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.
“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”
The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it released just the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Mattmiller declined to comment to the Observer, and Ferguson’s office didn’t respond to the publication. Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to Washington Needs to Compete, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive. GeekWire has contacted the group and the governor’s office for comment.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records , including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”
Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”
It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.
The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.
In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall , up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.
Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website , Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.
The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.
The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

articles.title: Seattle Stations Lead the Way on Light Rail Ridership
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Light rail ridership has been surging in the wake of the expansion of the 2 Line across Lake Washington on March 28 . The 1 Line now stretches from Federal Way to Lynnwood, with the 2 Line effectively doubling service from the Chinatown-International District to Lynnwood.

Four-minute peak frequencies in this overlapping segment are a major driver of ridership gains. Daily boardings remain above 160,000 even as the busy summer season has cooled. Gains in the Eastside portion of the light rail network have been less dramatic.

Due to construction defects and delays on the floating bridge portion of the 2 Line route, Sound Transit altered its plan and opened an Eastside-only "starter line" segment in 2024. That line extended to Downtown Redmond in spring 2025 and peaked just shy of 11,000 daily riders that summer, before fading over the fall and winter.

The extension of the 2 Line across the lake this spring has swelled ridership up to their summer 2025 peaks once more, but not significantly higher. The South Bellevue to Downtown Redmond segment averaged about 14,000 daily boardings in June, for example, but 11,330 in August after the World Cup ridership bump had subsided.

The 2 Line is almost assuredly garnering most of its ridership in its westside portion, from Seattle to Lynnwood. The caveat being we don't know for certain since Sound Transit told The Urbanist that it does not yet have the capability of separating 2 Line ridership from 1 Line ridership at the stations where both lines stop.

"Per our stats team, we do not currently have the ability to separate out 1 and 2 Line ridership in the core, but it is something the team is actively working on," Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said in an email. "We do not yet have a two 2 Line only whole system daily ridership number."

For the stations serving only the 2 Line, Sound Transit's ridership dashboard shows that Downtown Bellevue is leading the way, with South Bellevue in second. Downtown Bellevue averaged 2,541 daily boardings in August, while South Bellevue tallied 1,924, driven by its 1,500-stall parking garage.

Downtown Redmond is in third with just over 1,600 daily boardings, while Judkins Park (in Seattle) and Mercer Island fill out the top five. The 2 Line station struggling most for ridership is East Main, which managed just 480 daily riders in August.

Nearly every station west of Lake Washington is pulling in more ridership than even the busiest Eastside station. The exception is Rainier Beach, Kent Des Moines, and Star Lake, which are each below 2,500 daily boardings.
Westlake Station amassed 19,458 daily boardings in August, garnering more ridership than the entire East Link – the 12 stations served only by the 2 Line rather than both lines.

Eight of the top 10 stations for ridership are in Seattle. SeaTac's airport station (the second most-ridden) and Federal Way Downtown (in tenth) join the top 10 list. Seattle's top nine most-ridden stations all benefited from 2 Line expansion, which roughly doubled train frequencies, enticing more riders.

Since 1 Line and 2 Line ridership is currently lumped together in agency data (at least in overlapping stations) we don't know exactly how much of the load that the 2 Line is carrying at those stations.

The 1 Line is operating with a mix of four-car and three-car trains, while the 2 Line is typically two-car trains; so, the capacity of the 1 Line is greater. But riders traveling within the overlapping segment are likely to take whichever train comes first, which is effectively a coinflip when both are at eight-minute headways.

The lack of line-specific ridership data at Sound Transit could hinder the agency's ability to optimize its service patterns. However, a spokesperson did frame a solution to track the ridership by line, rather than in the aggregate only, as imminent.

The data shows a massive share of the agency's ridership passes through its top 10 busiest stations. The pattern has been fairly consistent in recent months, with about 65% of ridership happening in the top 10, versus just 35% in the remaining 16 stations in the corridor.

The largest ridership jump from August to September was at Shoreline South, which saw a 25% increase from just over 2,800 to just over 3,500 daily riders. This is likely the fall bus service change at work, and the increasing opportunity for bus-rail transfers after it – Route 522 now heads to Shoreline South instead of continuing along SR 522 to the University of Washington's Seattle campus, which means 522 riders headed to and from campus now hop a train in Shoreline. Another boost could be tied to the leasing up of new apartment buildings added near the station .
Federal Way was also a gainer in September, adding about 400 daily boardings and leapfrogging Roosevelt to become the ninth-busiest station for the month.

Meanwhile, the biggest ridership drops from August to September were at Stadium and Westlake. Stadium is yoked to the whims of sports fans and event schedules, and waning interest in the Seattle Mariners baseball team as their playoff odds evaporated must have hurt ridership totals. The drop of nearly 2,000 daily boardings at Westlake is more mysterious, but perhaps tied to a slowing of the tourism season. Sea-Tac Airport also saw a drop of roughly 1,000 daily boardings, in alignment with this hypothesis.

Overall, Sound Transit is largely sustaining ridership from its June peak during the height of World Cup fervor. In September, the 1 Line corridor came in just shy of 150,000 daily boardings, while the 2 Line hit nearly hitting 15,000 daily boardings in its exclusive segment.
Systemwide, September's ridership total is indeed down, but only moderately from the 178,264 daily boardings highwater park in June.
What the trend will be in months ahead is an interesting question.

Sound Transit does not have any big light rail openings planned for nearly a decade, with West Seattle Link and Tacoma Dome Link extensions expected to come online in 2035, barring further delays. The Graham Street infill station could be a small boost around 2031.

And given the lack of housing development near the station, the recently inaugurated Pinehurst infill station isn't likely to move the needle much on systemwide ridership, at least in the near term. Starting in 2028, the rollout of Sound Transit's Stride bus rapid transit system could add a boost via bus-to-rail transfers, but impact will likely be modest.

Since Sound Transit torrid pace of light rail expansion is hitting a lull, light rail ridership growth will need to be organic – likely built on adding homes and jobs near existing stations and attracting more riders through consistent service quality.

Part of the decline from the June peak could be attributed to the agency's going from a month of nearly flawless execution to a period with several major service disruption and hiccups . Who can blame would-be riders for hopping on a bike or scooter or hailing a cab on days when significant disruptions occur?

The good news is that cities up and down the line are generally aiming to add housing near their stations – albeit to varying results . Sound Transit has also pledged improvements to maintenance and how it handles disruptions, hoping to lessen the sting and keep riders trusting light rail is a reliable way to get where they need go.
Even without major expansions in the near-term horizon, Sound Transit ridership appears to be trending in the upward direction all the same.

articles.title: Beabamania
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: The day before the final show of the North American leg of her Powerlines Tour, British singer-songwriter Beatrice Laus, better known by her stage name beabadoobee, put out a request to her fans on social media: “HALLOWEEN SHOW last show of US tour in seattle tmrw dress up 😋”

And dress up they did: Harlequin clowns, fuzzy Garfields, and shivering angels lined up in the autumn evening chill outside Climate Pledge Arena. The fanbase skewed young. Everywhere you looked, an army of beabawannabes posed for photos in furry boots, short shorts, camo, military caps, and cargo pants in an attempt to imitate their idol.

The night started off strong with a set from San Francisco-based “nu-gaze” musician Natalie R. Lu, aka Wisp, who rose to TikTok fame in April 2023 with her viral single “Your Face,” which she recorded using a pair of Apple earbuds with no prior music production experience. Her band walked out to the Phantom of the Opera theme. “I’m not going to lie, I’m really feeling myself in this costume,” Lu said, in a goth Little Red Riding Hood ensemble complete with a fur-trimmed crimson velvet cloak, satin corset mini dress, and black boots. She sang into a mic adorned with a raven atop a stand festooned with spiders and cobwebs, while her band performed dressed as Stan and Kenny from South Park, a zombie, and a duck.

Wisp is a fitting name for the project: Lu’s ethereal, evanescent soundscapes and whispery vocals reminded me of the icy glitter of a frozen tundra. Her wistful, haunting walls of sound wrapped the dark venue as plumes of fake fog billowed from the stage. Between songs, she took bites of a croissant. “This has become one of my favorite songs to perform on this tour,” Lu said before launching into the soft acoustic guitar track “All i need.” The crowd erupted into cheers when she brought out her famous black Hello Kitty guitar . She ended with “Your Face,” pointing into the crowd at a fan as she delivered the line “I see your face.”

Before beabadoobee’s set, anticipation crackled through the arena as the sound of buzzing powerlines played over speakers. The set evoked a deserted highway, complete with a pylon, glowing powerlines, a streetlight, a divider, yellow painted lines, reflective pavement markers, and tufts of grass sprouting from rocky terrain. Beabadoobee wrote her fourth studio album Pylon while touring for her 2024 album This Is How Tomorrow Moves . The album gets its title from the pylon towers and powerlines she’d gaze out the window while homesick, a symbol of isolation and connection at the same time: “At least we’re connected / like a pylon on the open road.”

At last, beabadoobee and her band took the stage in skeleton costumes and ghoulish black face paint scars—Laus paired hers with baggy black cargo pants and combat boots. They opened with “Sun Has Set,” a punchy, blistering track: “When I say, ‘We’ll never be friends’ / I mean, we’ll never pretend / Fuck that, you can never run back to me now.”

Before playing the Pylon title track, Laus explained that she wrote the album about how much she was struggling on the 2024 tour and how she’d never imagined she would “play venues of this size.” “I did this as a joke,” she said, “and now it’s my life, and I wouldn’t do anything else.” She got her start in 2017, when she released her music under the name she had invented for a finsta account, and it stuck.

Laus sang the lyrics, “And I love you / It’s pouring in a place that I don’t know the name / But you’re always worth the wait” with bruised longing. Her sinuous voice had the ability to simultaneously convey heartache, infatuation, rage, loneliness, and pining, recalling Dolores O’Riordan with its potency and purity of emotion. Chugging, fuzzed-out guitars evoked the sensation of flying down a highway while staring out the window, building to a high-voltage crescendo as the powerlines flashed. I thought of Glen Campbell’s “Wichita Lineman,” another song about urgent yearning and electricity: “I hear you singin’ in the wire / I can hear you through the whine / And the Wichita lineman / Is still on the line.”

Moments of levity broke up all that melancholy. On the song “Take a Bite” (produced by hitmaker Rick Rubin and beabadoobee guitarist Jacob Bugden for This Is How Tomorrow Moves ), she exuded daring, defiance, and playfulness, bouncing around the stage and grinning. The crowd jumped up and down to the “la la la” chorus of the upbeat, cathartic “Nothing to Prove,” written in collaboration with Hayley Williams.

The September release of Pylon marked the adoption of an edgier, grungier new sound for beabadoobee, incorporating ’90s alt, radio rock, and Midwest emo influences and enlisting Williams, Pinegrove’s Evan Stephens Hall, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates as collaborators. Laus picked up a pink guitar and screamed, “I fucking love this song!” before launching into “Switchblade,” which channeled “Seether” by Veruca Salt, one of her favorite bands.

By contrast, some of beabadoobee’s earlier, more well-known songs felt almost incongruous with the grittier new material. Laus was inspired to write music after hearing Kimya Dawson’s songs on the Juno soundtrack, and that twee sweetness shines through in her older work. The audience squealed, swayed, and sang along to her hit debut single “Coffee,” which went viral on YouTube in 2017 and blew up even more after it was sampled on Canadian rapper ​​Powfu’s TikTok-popular 2019 song “Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head).” A group of teens behind me screeched at eardrum-splitting decibels the entire time, like they were front row at a Beatles concert during peak Beatlemania.

Though Laus expressed nothing but gratitude for her fans and played many of the songs that helped introduce them to her, I couldn’t help but wonder if she resents the staggering popularity of “Coffee” and the pressure to conform to her poppier earlier style. “I’m not going to lie, it was overwhelming… I kinda hated it. I hated more people knowing about the first song I’d ever written and not my others. I was so stubborn but I grew into it and accepted that’s just how life works. I was extremely grateful for its existence and it’s only given me more opportunities,” she told The Basement in 2020.

Nevertheless, like Pylon itself, the dynamic show nailed the bittersweet balance between nostalgia and angst. Songs like “Radio,” “Pictures of Us,” and the unreleased acoustic song “The Road,” which recalled Simon & Garfunkel, captured the driftless sense of an endless road trip against a backdrop with visuals of powerlines draped across a sky and trucks zooming along the highway. For the track “Powerlines,” Lau climbed the pylon onstage and performed while perched on it, and during “Satellite,” she picked up an old-school corded phone mounted on the set’s streetlamp and sang into the receiver: “Hold my breath until the dial tone / Ring, ring, ring to bring you back to me.”

At times, I picked up snatches of post-Britpop and garage rock influences á la the Strokes (Laus is heavily inspired by the band and covered their song “The Adults Are Talking” in 2022). I could feel the DNA of the music I grew up with embedded in her songs. An unbearable nostalgia for something I couldn’t quite name—for an earlier time that I can never return to and wouldn’t if I could, full of agony and bliss—made my chest ache. And for just a moment, amid all the screaming teens pogoing in Halloween costumes, I felt like I was there again.
The post Beabamania appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project . It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.
The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena , as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.
Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe , writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize , Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet , a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.
Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.
Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.
The second runner-up , Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.
His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.
Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.
All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

articles.title: Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Powerlattice , a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.
The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.
AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.
“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou , Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.
“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: From gunfire to combative arrests: How the Seattle Police Department talks about East Precinct crime is changing
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: (Source: CHS analysis of SPD Significant Incident Reports )

As Capitol Hill crime trends are shifting as part of City Hall priorities to increase public safety downtown, the way the public is informed about the Seattle Police Department’s day to day enforcement, arrests, and challenges across the city and in the East Precinct is also changing.

CHS reported here this summer on a key shift as SPD and Seattle Fire have now mostly fully encrypted their dispatch and emergency radio transmissions, cutting off real-time public and scanner access to tactical and operational channels.
Other public channels documenting 911 incidents in the city are also shifting.

One suddenly more important outlet with the radio channel near-blackout are SPD’s Significant Incident Reports . Prepared by each precinct for daily command briefings, the department has regularly published a selected stream of SIR updates for over six years now after beginning the practice following the onset of the pandemic and the civil unrest surrounding CHOP .

The stream of briefs signed-off on and approved by precinct commanders for publication provide information on individual incidents and arrests. They are also revealing of shifting priorities in information at SPD.

While the Seattle Police Department has drastically curtailed SIR public blotter updates citywide, East Precinct’s totals have taken an opposite path, not only expanding its share of published reports, but transforming the precinct’s Significant Incident Reports stream into a platform focused on officer hazards and physical resistance during arrests.

Across the department, blotter publication has slowed to all-time lows in 2026. Citywide postings dropped nearly 25% year-to-date, falling from a 2021 peak of 5.4 daily incident reports to just 2.4. The South and Southwest precincts drive much of this pullback, paring down their posts to focus primarily on gunfire and shell casing recoveries, with shootings accounting for around 40% of their recent posts.
East Precinct moved in the opposite direction. From 2021 through 2023, East accounted for just 14.9% of all citywide SIR entries, ranking last among SPD’s five precincts.
That came even as downtown enforcement pushed crime eastward , with Capitol Hill recording 780 additional offenses by 2025 and passing downtown for the city’s highest raw crime count.
In 2025 and 2026, East’s share of the blotter also surged — to 20.8%, overtaking both South and Southwest. A bigger change in the East reports is their nature.

Instead of cataloging major neighborhood violence — confirmed gunfire reports dropped from 28.3% of East entries during 2021–2023 down to 16.9% recently — the blotter has shifted toward documenting the occupational hazards and physical friction officers encounter while making arrests.

East now leads the entire city in publicizing physical threats to personnel. Over 12% of recent East posts, peaking at nearly 14% in 2025, detail suspects physically fighting officers during handcuffing, spitting in officers’ faces, brandishing weapons at patrol, or facing felony assault and obstruction charges. These physical confrontations frequently emerge during lower-level disorder calls, including retail trespass, public urination, and crisis detentions.
Arrests are also highlighted. Reports emphasizing suspect custody leaped from 36.3 to 46.1%.

Even as monthly crime across Capitol Hill and First Hill began cooling in late summer 2026, the East Precinct information flow has held firm, making the precinct’s SIR updates a record of enforcement hazards and showcasing the combative arrests and physical resistance officers face.

As for what is happening day to day across the neighborhoods of the East Precinct, sources like the Seattle Fire real-time 911 logs remain. A growing array of for–pay, non-public services like the Citizen app are also flowering. Citizen was originally launched as “Vigilante” and is backed by prominent Silicon Valley venture capital firms, high-profile angel investors, and growth funds if you have any question about the goals behind it.

As Seattle’s public safety communications contract behind encrypted radios and reduced blotter output, the day-to-day picture of policing in the East Precinct could largely become a reflection of command selection. While commercial apps monetize access to 911 monitoring, SPD’s official updates have narrowed their lens.

The city’s news gatherers have weathered change before and CHS is finding new ways to keep up with — and dig up — crime and emergency news. We also have access to a unique and powerful resource — you:

articles.title: Route 40 Upgrades Finally Reach Finish Line, Despite Business Opposition
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle and King County officials cut the ribbon on a suite of upgrades to Metro's workhorse Route 40 on Thursday – transit speed, reliability, and access improvements that have been in the works for the better part of a decade. The changes benefit around 9,000 daily transit riders traveling between Downtown Seattle, Fremont, Ballard, Crown Hill, and Northgate, but several key elements had faced significant opposition from business owners along the route.

Upgrades include three miles of business access and transit (BAT) lanes, targeted at some of the 40's biggest pinch points including stretches through the heart of Ballard, on either side of the Fremont Bridge, and along Westlake Avenue N. Sixteen bus stops were upgraded and more than 6,000 feet of new sidewalks were installed, with new crosswalks and curb ramps up and down the corridor.

"One of the busiest routes in King County – top five actually – has become faster, safer, and easier to use," King County Executive Girmay Zahilay said Thursday. "And for our riders, that means getting a little bit of time back and having a ride that they can count on. This is definitely worth celebrating and sharing gratitude with all of the teams who had so much to do with these improvements, as well as the community members who advocated for this."

Utility work that was able to happen at the same time as construction, including the replacement of 200 feet of water main, stretched out the implementation timeline, as did planning delays and budgetary turmoil. Backers of the 2015 Move Seattle Levy (which funded the project) had hoped to open the Route 40 upgrades as a RapidRide line in 2023, but ultimately scaled back the plan and abandoned the RapidRide branding in 2018 due to a budget crunch and worse federal transit funding outlook under the Trump administration 1.0.

Dedicated road space for buses is what drew the most organized opposition, which continued through the start of construction . In 2021, The Urbanist first reported pushback on the project's initial design coming from Eugene Wasserman, President of the North Seattle Industrial Association.

Wasserman has long been involved in the fight over completing the Missing Link of the Burke-Gilman Trail along Shilshole Way NW through Ballard and was one of the main opponents of the 2015 Levy to Move Seattle, which funded about 30% of the annual budget of the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). In opposing the Route 40 project, he cited potential impacts on routes used by freight trucks due to reallocating street space.

"It appears to the Maritime/Industrial community that SDOT is willing to sacrifice the viability of maritime/industrial businesses and their employees so that Amazon workers can get to their offices 5 minutes earlier," Wasserman wrote at the time. "Removing the number of traffic lanes the project does will have a substantial impact on our maritime/industrial businesses and will assist in the increasing gentrification of our industrial area."

While that opposition was initially confined to the freight community, it quickly expanded, with business groups in Fremont and Ballard also raising concerns. A 2023 letter signed by Pete Hanning, the head of the Fremont Chamber of Commerce and Mike Stewart, head of the Ballard Alliance, framed the project as out-of-date, citing a reduction in ridership on the Route 40 compared to pre-pandemic levels. Today, the Route 40 is one of the most popular routes in the Metro network, seeing only slightly less usage than the nearby D Line.

"SDOT did not conduct a thorough existing conditions study to identify the specific areas where improvements are needed, let alone the consequences that will result with respect to side-street congestion and overloaded vehicle queues, reliable movement of freight, and increased idling that will result in excessive carbon emissions," the 2023 letter stated.

Two separate traffic analysis studies were conducted on the changes, in response to the issues raised by project opponents and amplified by former Seattle City Council President Sara Nelson. Nelson came out against the bus lanes in 2023 and threatened to kill the transit project through the council budget process in 2024. In 2025, Nelson lost her reelection bid by 25 points to progressive nonprofit leader Dionne Foster.

Business opposition continued into 2025, as some design changes were made to respond to community concerns. SDOT relocated a bus stop location in Fremont and redesigned a new crosswalk at Westlake Avenue N and Halladay Street to reduce impacts on a nearby business. Most notably, the City of Seattle committed to piloting a new concept for the city, a freight-and-bus (FAB) lane along Westlake Avenue N to potentially mitigate some impacts to truck traffic.
Despite those changes, signs reading "Route 40 Plan: We Can Do Better" kept popping up along the route as the project was getting ready to start construction, as organized opposition continued.

Throughout its planning and construction, the project received significant support from multimodal transportation advocates, specifically Ballard Fremont Green Streets (BFG), previously known as Ballard-Fremont Greenways. An email campaign started by the group attempted to counter the opposition, a tactic that certainly helped the Route 40 upgrades to arrive at their ribbon cutting largely unscathed.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, who had been involved in the fight over upgrading the Route 40 as head of the Transit Rider's Union before being elected to lead the city, clearly took joy in being able to mark the occasion.

"These kinds of meaningful improvements matter as they make a difference in the everyday lives of residents of our city, and that is why I've also directed us SDOT to continue this trend to keep making our existing bus routes better at the same time as we launch new ones," Wilson said. "And so, really looking forward to continuing that work."

Zahilay told the crowd Thursday that initial data from Metro on the upgrades shows a 11% improvement in travel time for the Route 40 between Fremont and Ballard, which translates to 90 seconds saved on every bus trip, on average.

"Many of my neighbors and my friends rely on the 40 to work, to visit friends and family, to go to big events, to go shopping," Jason Weill, an advocate with Ballard Fremont Green Streets, said. "One BFG member told me that she commutes using the 40, and she used to deal with long delays, sitting through the bus [waiting] through multiple light cycles. But now the cars that used to block the lane have made way for busses."

But the improvements to the public realm extend beyond benefits to the bus riders themselves, with Lydia Heard of the Fremont Neighborhood Council noting that creating transit lanes has turned Fremont into a more walkable neighborhood.

"The reconfiguration of 35th at Fremont Place has a calming effect and transforms that corner into a more welcoming public space," Heard said. "But perhaps the biggest transformation is where the dedicated bus lane reduced [N] 36th to one general travel lane in each direction. This stretch of street, lined with popular businesses and often teeming with foot traffic, feels quieter and calmer most of the day. It is a much more enjoyable walking experience, and it is easier to cross the street. I think this is what we want for our community."
