articles.title: Bellevue's Transportation Funding Debate Pivots Around Safety
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Competing visions for the future of Bellevue's transportation system were put on full display this week at a final public hearing before adoption of the city's next two-year budget. As city leaders contemplate how to utilize several new revenue streams for transportation projects, the big question is how heavily Bellevue will invest in multimodal traffic safety upgrades that reduce deaths and injuries and make it easier to get around without a car.

With a new 0.1% sales tax and a new $20 vehicle license fee likely on deck in Bellevue, the question of utilizing those dollars for safety upgrades had already been top-of-mind during council discussions over the course of this year. But the discussion took on an increased level of urgency after a driver struck and killed 57-year-old James Rupert William Phillips while he was riding his bike at Bellevue Way SE and SE 30th Street on October 15.

Phillips was killed during a planned maintenance closure of the I-90 trail, with a detour directing anyone trying to get between Bellevue and Mercer Island to city streets. According to an initial police report, Phillips, a Newcastle resident, was crossing Bellevue Way when he was struck in one of Bellevue Way's inside lanes. The driver remained at the scene, Bellevue Police Department reported .

Crossing Bellevue Way in this spot, which doesn't include any crossing infrastructure, would be a tempting choice for anyone trying to get to the westbound I-90 trail without having to backtrack from all the way from 112th Avenue NE.

While decisions around the trail detour rested with King County as part of the North Mercer Island/Enatai Sewer Upgrade Project , the incident has thrown a spotlight on conditions on Bellevue's arterial streets.

Earlier this month, Bellevue councilmembers got a full breakdown on potential funding scenarios that would allocate more than $100 million in new funding across the Eastside's largest city over the next decade. Under the most ambitious scenario, which includes the 0.1% sales tax on top of the vehicle license fees, bicycle and pedestrian safety projects would see 28% of the city's total transportation spending through 2036. Neighborhood safety projects including traffic calming would see an additional 13%.

At Tuesday's hearing, councilmembers heard from Bellevue residents, workers, and visitors about whether to tweak or maintain those funding levels. Over recent weeks, signs have been popping up around Bellevue reading "no car tab tax" and "don't raise sales taxes." A fair share of speakers at the hearing told the council that new revenue tools should go to the voters, but most touching on transportation urged the city to stick to this new proposed baseline or go even further.

"I appreciate, value, and am very grateful for Bellevue adopting Vision Zero goals. We clearly need to do more," Bellevue resident Elaine White said, referencing the tragic Bellevue Way incident. "Please adopt scenario 3 in the 2027-2028 transportation budget. It funds more speed cameras, more improvements for vulnerable users and slower speeds. Yes, it will cost each household an additional $6 a month. Fellow residents of Bellevue, what might the life of your loved one be worth protecting? I'm happy to pay $6 per month for safer streets."

One area of emphasis was the "major projects" category, which would see most of the $40 million in new spending go toward getting a $74.8 million roadway project through the BelRed neighborhood across the finish line. The Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project would reconnect a segment of the street grid with sidewalks and protected bike lanes, but at an enormous cost – bringing a roadway through one of the neighborhood's only planned park spaces.

"In the last two and a half years since the light rail station was opened, nothing was made to improve pedestrian or bicycle access to the light rail station. During the last five years, we asked repeatedly for mid-block crossing on our street, and we heard no results," Crossroads resident Alex Kon said. "While then transportation department for years can't find money to fix those glaring safety and accessibility gaps, it suggests to spend $75 million dollars to build new arterial road nobody is asking for, and to add insult to injury, this road will go right through the park, so it will split into halves instead of improving connectivity for people who live there or who visit the park."

The Grand Connection Crossing , Bellevue's plan to construct a bike and pedestrian bridge across I-405 between Downtown and the Wilburton neighborhood, was also a target of public comments. While the crossing is set to receive around 10% of revenue from the sales tax increase, those dollars had been set to come from Bellevue's general fund, freeing up dollars that can be spent more broadly.

"In this budget, our central request is to keep the Grand Connection Crossing funded and moving forward," Patrick Bannon, President and CEO of the Bellevue Downtown Association. "Connecting Downtown, Wilburton, Eastrail will make it easier to reach jobs, businesses, homes, places to shop, places to eat. It will help attract the next generation of private investment and support the next wave of housing growth in our city."
While the city's business community is fully on board with the idea of building the Grand Connection Crossing, the project has its detractors.

"Responsible government should address current problems such as traffic congestion first, which would be [a] much more reasonable cost than the current proposal. Instead, the most pressing concerns of the transportation department, from the beginning, the past several years, seems to have been on serving cyclists by narrowing lanes and later by building the Grand Connection," Bridle Trails resident Anne Coughlin said. "It seems that the few blocks from 112 to 116[th] are a great barrier to those who wish to cross it on bicycle, as though it were the 3.6 million miles separating sub-Saharan Africa from the north, the Himalayas, or the Amazonian rainforest."

But the Grand Connection Crossing is far from the only transportation project that the business community is advocating for. Tony Sprague, Public Policy Manager for the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce, noted that their group's support for the funding package is contingent on no reductions for "vehicular capacity" projects, and has also requested that additional revenue beyond current sales tax projections be put into the "underperforming intersection" fund.

The vehicle mobility program already includes three planned intersection widenings, at SE 8th St and 114th Ave SE, NE 12th St and 116th Ave NE, and 148th Ave NE and NE 8th St, for a total cost of $24.5 million. That's more funding for three projects than the entire neighborhood mobility program would receive in new funding over the course of a full decade.

Whether any additional funding can be diverted into the types of transportation modes that Bellevue will need to grow sustainably over the coming decades – walking, biking and transit – remains to be seen in the coming weeks. Following council deliberations on November 3 and 10, a finalized budget is expected to be adopted by the Bellevue Council on November 17.

articles.title: State Supreme Court Candidate Sean O’Donnell Says He Supports Reproductive Rights, Local Advocates Aren’t Convinced
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: Abortion rights win elections. With days left until the November 3 general election, that could be a late-breaking problem for Washington State Supreme Court candidate Sean O’Donnell, who is running in an increasingly contentious race against Washington State Court of Appeals Judge Ian Birk. O’Donnell, who has been endorsed by several Democratic legislative districts, but also the Washington State Republican Party and has received financial backing from conservative PACs, told The Stranger he respects laws supporting abortion rights. But he never filled out an endorsement questionnaire from either Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates or Northwest Reproductive Equity Action, the state’s leading reproductive rights advocacy groups, whose approval indicates candidates’ support for the issue. Both groups have endorsed Birk. (So has The Stranger Election Control Board .)

Now, O’Donnell’s camp is contending that their candidate does support reproductive rights, but simply didn’t follow through on the endorsement process. “Sean fully supports reproductive healthcare,” says the judge’s political consultant, Stephen Paolini. O’Donnell himself says the same thing. But according to Paolini, the campaign received a Planned Parenthood endorsement questionnaire in April that asked how O’Donnell would rule on specific issues, so the campaign didn’t respond. In Washington, judicial positions are nonpartisan, and candidates must be careful about being too political lest it show bias. Paolini also said that he had tried to contact Northwest Reproductive Equity Action’s lobbyist, but that the organization hadn’t reached out to the campaign directly.

Both groups dispute this account. According to Courtney Normand, the Washington State director at Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, the organization’s endorsement questionnaire for judicial candidates is crafted to be “mindful of the judicial code of ethics and conduct” and, as such, specifically does not ask how candidates would rule on certain issues. She said other judicial candidates had filled it out without issue. “The chief justice of the Supreme Court returned our questionnaire, no problem,” she says, referring to Debra Stephens, who is running for re-election.

While it’s possible O’Donnell’s camp simply made a mistake, says Normand, “I can tell you, the judges that we endorsed, we had a lot of engagement from. We didn’t have to chase them down to participate in our process.”

That process is generally familiar to political candidates in Washington, especially those looking to publicly affirm their support for reproductive rights. It’s unusual for pro-choice candidates to opt out.

When you’re running for office in Washington, it’s common knowledge that Planned Parenthood and Northwest Reproductive Equity Action are key organizations from which to seek an endorsement, said Sen. June Robinson, a member of the Washington State Senate’s Health & Long-Term Care Committee. “Those are the two organizations that, as a candidate, everybody knows that they’re a benchmark for those issues,” she says, adding that in a state like Washington, where there is a long history of affirming reproductive rights, “It’s very strange to hide on that issue.”

According to political manager Paul Dillon, Northwest Reproductive Equity Action’s candidate questionnaire is publicly available online, and could have been accessed by O’Donnell’s campaign at any time. “They could have gone online and submitted it,” says Dillon. “They did not. And so that’s on them.”

Dillon said that O’Donnell’s opponent Birk reached out to the organization ahead of the endorsement process, and even traveled to Spokane to meet with Dillon personally. “That showed a lot of intention on his part and how much he does deeply care about the issues of choice and access to abortion, and that spoke volumes to me,” says Dillon.

Birk confirmed his meeting with Dillon and early interest in Northwest Reproductive Equity Action’s endorsement process. He said he didn’t recall anything unusual about the candidate questionnaires, or the expectation that candidates take the initiative to seek out endorsements, which are especially important in these non-partisan judicial races since they are one of the few avenues to connect with voters.

“There’s certainly nothing that would prevent a candidate from participating in this process,” he says, adding that O’Donnell’s lack of engagement came as a surprise. “I think that the focus on healthcare access, healthcare equity, and healthcare affordability is just very important in society.” In his previous career as a personal injury attorney, Birk often advocated for clients seeking insurance coverage or disability benefits, or otherwise navigating major barriers to all kinds of health care. “This issue does come before the court,” he says.
Paolini said the opposite was true of abortion, specifically: that access is “incredibly settled law” in Washington. “There is zero threat here,” he says. “Sean supports reproductive healthcare.”

For Normand, that was a red flag, given national attacks on abortion rights and efforts to limit access even in states with protective policies. “Anyone who is on the bench in Washington state knows that attacks are being lobbed at us all the time,” she says. “And as one of the nation’s leading reproductive rights states, we’re a target for anything the other side can come up with to bring to court. So not only do I think that’s wrong, I think it’s alarming that they’re not taking it more seriously.”

articles.title: The Stranger’s Noise Complaint: Intisaar Jubran
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Welcome to Noise Complaint, The Stranger ‘s new audio and video music podcast featuring live performances right here at The Stranger HQ. Streamed live and released every other Friday, we invite a great band, musician, or wonderfully weird act to perform. Tune in, discover something new, and support art in your city.
Palestinian-American Singer-Songwriter Intisaar Jubran

Nationwide, the singer-songwriter field is, sadly, peopled with more mediocrities than stars. So when one comes along with the instrumental deftness, lyrical gravitas, and expressive voice of Intisaar Jubran, you gotta pay respect and attention. From her first single, 2009’s “Tamarind” on, the Palestinian-American’s been creating tough and tender folk-pop, displaying a delicate fluidity on acoustic guitar and singing with a warm radiance.

On the 2012 Intisaar EP and 2015 debut album Borrowed Ground , Intisaar developed a pensive, orchestral sound that rewards deep listening, with help from cellist Natalie Mae Hall (who’s worked with Macklemore & Ryan Lewis and the Eagles, among others). On the mic, Intisaar possesses a Joni Mitchell-esque penchant for the unexpected chord and vocal leap and dip and, at crucial moments, a Jeff Buckley-like flair for glossolalia.

Now a trio with the in-demand Greg Ferguson (Western War, Juno, etc.) behind the drum kit, this iteration of Intisaar makes its debut on Noise Complaint and will perform at Clock-Out Lounge on November 14 for the fourth edition of the Radio Gaza fundraiser benefiting Heal Palestine ( radiogaza.org ). articles.title: Tender and Tedious (Sometimes Ecstatic)
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: There are only two days remaining—today and tomorrow—to see Melissa Messer’s paintings at Spectrum Fine Art , a gallery tucked in Madrona along a commercial strip that’s currently being inundated by a fury of autumnal color.

Hanging in the gallery window, visible from the street, is a small painting titled A Pair of Roman Dogs . It’s a mere 12 inches square, but I can’t stop thinking about the pathos packed into such a diminutive image. Against a backdrop of deep, murky olive, one of the dogs pops, rendered in lemony yellow and shades of acrid, bilious burnt gold. The shadows across its face are formed by a series of spare brushstrokes (you can count them: seven) in ochre and mustard. A single, steady brushstroke in muted brown forms the mouth, turning up at the edges in a slight smile. I think it’s a smile?

The second hound, a dusty, earthen mauve teetering on aubergine, sits behind the first in a gesture like a caress, its head and snout resting on the other’s back. Its hand—because this is where the dog seems almost to become human—rests on the golden shoulder of its companion. A cool blue blush of light glances off both.

The image is tender, conveying something like belonging and companionship. Yet the acidity of the color strips it of any saccharine, doggy-in-the-window sentimentality. Whether it contains some deeper meaning is almost beside the point. As an exercise in art for art’s sake, it’s a really fucking satisfying painting.

Interestingly, A Pair of Roman Dogs is the only piece in the show of new works currently hanging at Spectrum that features non-human figures. The rest depict human bodies in various configurations, either reposed or arrested mid-motion against swaths of color that are constantly surprising in their fresh weirdness. There’s really no other way to put it. Like the jarring icy cobalt and ink black of Night Diver No. 2, Search, and Rescue , or the more mellow but still-bracing blues and browns of Ice Age and Landlocked . (You can see them all here .)

Part of Messer’s brilliance lies in her use of color, which sometimes seems to turn the figures into foils for color play. And she embraces it, self-identitifying as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.”
To get deeper into her brain, I asked Messer a few questions about process and practice.

Walk me through the birth of a painting. Where does the process begin—with an image, a feeling, a relationship, a color, or something else? MESSER: It starts with a feeling in the body that becomes a theme. Like a pose I’m taking over and over in my life and I really get into the psychology and emotion of it. In early motherhood, I was bending over and kneeling constantly with a small child. It keeps your knees sore and compresses your lungs. It’s something you do to engage closer. It’s intense, tender, tedious, and at times ecstatic. Think of these poses as shapes—a Kneeler, a Diver—they become symbols for what? Humility, labor, surrender. But also devotion and service. A few years later, the theme is different. There is a persistent pause before getting up. Taking a beat for myself, like in Pre-War Champagne and Ice Age . These positions, when distilled and repeated, become symbols of resilience, repair, and needing to finish one bleeding thought.

What comes first: the figure or the color? MESSER: Figure! If my paintings were songs, the figures are the lyrics and the color is the music. I take figure shapes, and I think about all the ways they manifest somatically and I write music for those images. Which is to say, I compose harmonies, disharmonies, and rhythms through color to evoke the emotion.

How do you think about color’s relationship to emotion? Are you using it to elicit a particular feeling, or are you more interested in its purely optical effects? MESSER: Yeah, the color isn’t everything but it’s everything at first. It’s emotional and visceral. It’s the impact before you enter the painting. In my favorite paintings, I’m confronted with color that sets the tone before I enter. Not even in a loud way. But there is communication happening before your brain gets involved. I’m always after that impact moment before you dive in.

I love the description: as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.” What is it about Rothko’s work that works for you, and do you have a favorite piece? MESSER: Thanks for asking this. It changes all the time! Whatever it’s doing, it’s spiritual. I was born in Houston, not far from the Rothko Chapel. Rothko is the household name among a group of mid-century American colorists that includes Milton and March Avery. They are my North Stars for color work. I try to build from them. Matisse is the painter that made me want to be a painter. And Hilma af Klint showed me you can investigate meaning through color. Alice Neel showed me how to look at your friends without blinking.

What does “not blinking” mean, in practical terms? Neel painted the people in her life with a gaze that is both irreverent in its humor or lack of idealism, but also reverent in its intimacy and close-looking. I love this quality in relationships. It’s this feeling of being so close that it feels expansive. It’s a radical kind of intimacy. I paint my friends, we collaborate on physical experiences. We hold each other’s infants hours after birth. How does it show up pictorially? Well there’s a lot of empathy and deep seeing in the process. And I know that I couldn’t make paintings without it.

Speaking of your friends, who are the subjects in your paintings and how do you choose them? MESSER: Oh, what a treat to get to talk about Ruth! I only paint my close friends. But mostly, I paint Ruth Bryan. She’s a dancer, a therapist who works with intimacy and embodiment, and very recently a mother. My own mother has asked if paintings of Ruth are self-portraits and I think that is owed a little to our shared hair texture and high cheekbones, but mostly to Ruth’s talent as a physical communicator. She can inhabit my symbolic experience while expressing her own.

How do you work with her to develop those poses? And how much of a painting is determined before you begin versus discovered along the way? MESSER: I have these shapes I’m sketching all the time. I bring them to Ruth and we set them up like Pose A, Pose B, Pose C. And then we let the camera roll. She moves slowly through this sequencing and we find these transitional positions along the way that are off-kilter somehow and express something much closer to life while still maintaining a symbolic quality. I don’t want her to look like a statue. “The breath of life” is crucial even when I’m playing with abstraction or symbolism. Rather, especially then!

Your paintings hold a lot of tension between abstraction and physical presence, between flattened planes of color and the weight of a body. How does your interest in sculpture—and in antiquity, more broadly—inform your approach? MESSER: God, I love sculpture! In another life I’m a sculptor. In my head I am one. This is where Rothko’s color fields come in. I think of a figure like a sculpture and I try to take as few cuts as possible to give me the largest planes possible to make color fields on the body. Sometimes there’s a lot of tension in a shoulder or the core and I need to chisel down for that detail to communicate the emotion in the figure. But mostly I try to limit the cuts and expand the color. Sometimes this leads to full-on abstraction. I think of myself as a contemporary painter who works in that tension between the modern colorists who flattened everything and antiquity, which imbued everything with physicality and weight. I love heft. Hockney said “Without form there is nothing.” I get that.

And the dogs…who are they? What are they? Yes, ok the dogs, the outliers, the scamps. They are a Roman sculpture piece from the 2nd century found in the foot of Italy’s boot. I experiment with form and color ideas on abstract forms, blobby cylinders. But sometimes I use these dogs as a shorthand. What’s funny about them to me is that these Italian greyhounds don’t ring especially symbolic. The sculptor makes them almost human. There is something so compelling about their relationship.

articles.title: Goodbye, Captain Picard
articles.author: By Josh Flanders
paras: In July 2022, the Yorkshire Post asked Patrick Stewart if, like his character Jean-Luc Picard, he actually drank Earl Grey tea. No, he said. He preferred Yorkshire Gold. I immediately ordered a large box, and, truth be told, it is delicious. So last night, in remembrance of his life, I poured a cup of Yorkshire Gold, hot, read Shakespeare’s Sonnet 71 , and recalled the words of Enterprise captain Picard in Star Trek: Generations :
“Time is a companion who goes with us on the journey and reminds us to cherish every moment, because they’ll never come again. What we leave behind is not as important as how we lived.”

The best part of my sophomore year of college at the University of Wisconsin–Madison occurred every weeknight at midnight, when my closest friends arrived at my dorm room for a sacred ritual: watching Picard captain the starship USS Enterprise (NCC-1701-D) in the latest rerun of Star Trek: The Next Generation ( TNG ) , a show still on the air in 1991. We sat in ecstatic silence, candles lit, while Stewart presided on the bridge, his arm pointed toward the future, leading us through the universe and building bridges with other worlds. He imparted more than a lifetime of wisdom and listened intently to his crew’s needs and his own heart. It was the closest thing to a religious experience I’ve ever had.

So I was devastated to learn that Stewart passed on Wednesday. According to his spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, he’d died of Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. He was 86. Thankfully, Stewart had a “brief and poignant journey” with these terrible diseases, both of which afflicted my father for too many years. Stewart did not publicly reveal his diagnosis in life, so his loss feels sudden and poignant for those of us restless to see him reprise the role of X-Men’s Professor Charles Xavier in Avengers: Doomsday, in theaters December 18 .

The enormity of his talent and range was stunning. He captured the screen in roles both serious and lighthearted ( The Sheep Detectives , Robin Hood: Men in Tights , L.A. Story), commanded the stage ( Antony and Cleopatra and Macbeth in the West End, Waiting for Godot with his dear friend Ian McKellen on Broadway), won three Olivier Awards and a Grammy for Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf , and even cut it up with a raunchy stand-up routine at age 75.

But his deep humanity, relationship with the written word, and good-humored spontaneity touched my heart most. For five months during the pandemic, he entered our homes to recite a daily Shakespeare sonnet, opening our shuttered worlds to a renewed desire, a deep ache, and a celebratory beauty. His hopeful spirit and endlessly engaging, hilarious presence brought so many people, and aliens in the far reaches of the universe, to Shakespeare over the years, connecting us all to a shared humanity.

Members of the Improvised Shakespeare Company at iO Theater in Chicago, including creator Blaine Swen, often speak in hushed reverence about the first of many times Stewart joined them onstage for an unforgettable surprise performance. In American Theatre , Stewart recalled, “. . . When I first saw Improvised Shakespeare Company . . . in Chicago in January 2013, I was astonished and full of wonder. How can this be improvisation? I thought. How can it be for the first time?”

I had a similar surprise when I attended the Chicago Symphony Orchestra’s performance of Igor Stravinsky’s opera-oratorio Oedipus Rex in February 2010, only to discover Sir Patrick Stewart himself was narrating, in person!

Given who he was, his deep commitment to social justice was no surprise. Stewart championed arts education in schools, as well as organizations that advocate for survivors of domestic violence, such as Refuge . As a boy, he had watched his father, a veteran, return traumatized from World War II and abuse his mother while he looked on helplessly. “Violence against women is learned,” he said. “Each of us must examine—and change—the ways in which our own behavior might contribute to, enable, ignore or excuse all such forms of violence.” Stewart also stood with the queer community. After Ian McKellen came out as gay in 1988 , Stewart became a longstanding public patron of PFLAG.

But his greatest contribution to the world, in my opinion, is Picard in TNG (and later Star Trek: Picard ) . Through Gene Roddenberry’s vision, Stewart immortalized phrases that will perhaps be repeated into the 2360s: “Make it so!” “Engage!” “Earl Grey, hot,” and the greatest meme of all time, “Wesley!”

Entire doctoral theses could be written (and probably have been) about Picard’s impact. Yet at the end of the day, he was just damn sexy. Suddenly on our TV screens came this fascinating, bald, British man into our homes, reciting poetry, drinking tea, playing music, and wooing women of all species in the great legacy of James T. Kirk, and he did it with little bravado. Just a thoughtful mix of humility and confidence, inquisitiveness, and stubbornness in a burgundy Starfleet jumpsuit. And that Earl Grey is indeed hot.

Standing on the bridge of the USS Enterprise as the egalitarian captain of a multicultural and interspecies crew, the character of Picard was groundbreaking because he built bridges, figuratively and emotionally. From its first episode in 1987, near the end of the Reagan era, to its final episode in 1994, early in the Clinton era, TNG bridged a conservative, materialistic America with the idealism and hope for a more liberal, compassionate country. Boldly going where few TV shows had gone before, TNG was progressive and approached issues way before the culture could catch up, tackling gender (like the episode “The Outcast,” where Jonathan Frakes’s character of Riker has a relationship with Soren, a member of an androgynous race; addressing conversion therapy to a muddle of praise and critique from the LGBTQ+ community), xenophobia, feminism, race, artificial intelligence, conflict resolution, and, of course, the Prime Directive, which involves the morality of interfering with prewarp civilizations not yet able to travel the stars.

I took a fantastic folklore class at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where the teacher required us to watch TNG season 5, episode 2, “Darmok,” an episode that perfectly espouses Stewart’s oeuvre and includes a phrase any Trekkie would know: “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra. ”

In this episode, Picard encounters an alien starship captain, Dathon of the Tamarians, who communicates only in metaphors and allegories from their culture’s history and mythology. To help Picard understand the Tamarian language, Dathon brings Picard to the hostile planet of El-Adrel IV to fight an invisible monster. After great frustration and confusion, the determined Picard discovers that “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra” refers to a Tamarian fable in which two enemies work together to conquer a common foe. It clicks when Picard connects the tale to a story from his human culture, The Epic of Gilgamesh, which he recites. By the end of this episode, Picard enters Tamarian legend (“Picard and Dathon at El-Adrel” ), but I suggest you watch it for yourself .

Such selfless cooperation is often alien to our contemporary human culture, but TNG , and this episode in particular, imagines a future far beyond borders without being naively utopian. Many of Earth’s problems have been solved, and many new galactic problems have emerged, yet the show offers hope that all people—or beings as they may be—may continue to transcend their differences and find ways to come together under the stars.
But today, we mourn the loss of Captain Picard.
This story was originally published by our sister paper, Chicago Reader .

articles.title: I, Anonymous: Let Dogs Be Dogs
articles.author: Anonymous
paras: For the love of all things holy, the dog park is NOT your petting zoo.

If you have a dog, fine, bring your kid. I’ll make an exception. But check the gummy bears at the door. And for everyone’s safety and sanity, make sure your walking liabilities aren’t covered in PB&J and Goldfish dust.

My dog is a rescue. She has issues. She does NOT want you petting her head. EVER. AT ALL. She will react. No, she won’t bite, but she’ll scare the absolute shit out of you, your precious prince/princess/princex, and me.

Dogs at the park are already amped up and doing dog stuff. They’re not there for your entertainment or affection. Keep your hands to yourself, let dogs approach if they choose, and understand that no dog owes you affection—regardless of your age.

We’re here because it’s one of the few places my dog can run free with other unhinged dogs and just be a dog. I’m not here to supervise your kids or have some blond every-other-weekend dad lecture me about my dog’s behavior while making absolutely no effort to manage his own kid in the ONE PLACE designed for dogs to be dogs.

And if you don’t have a dog, do NOT bring your child for the “experience.” That’s not enrichment; it’s entitlement. People with no real experience around dogs wind up doing dumb shit like trying to cuddle a goddamn husky.
The dog park is for dogs. Let them have their fucking park.

articles.title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
articles.author:
<name>Tara Deans, Associate Professor of Biomedical Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/tara-deans-2724020"/>
paras: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “ The Last of Us ,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “ SpongeBob SquarePants .”

These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close.

I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.

Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making.
The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus , Ophiocordyceps , which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”

The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin.

Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip . After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again.

How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers , but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.

The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus , showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it.

Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved.

That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus.
Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior.

The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa , uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it.

Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed.

Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.

Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.
Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. Toxoplasma gondii can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats.

While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even become attracted to cat odors . This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.

These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator.

There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.

So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them.
Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.
Tara Deans receives funding from the National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
articles.author:
<name>Drew Kurlowski, Associate Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/drew-kurlowski-2312625"/>
paras: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.

The story has driven calls for prosecutions , lawsuits and state action . But as a political scientist who studies election law , I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.
For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state.

In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “ Spurious Ticket .”
By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.
As observers in Alaska have noted , recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move.

In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy , no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.
Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message.

In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.”

Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986.
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.
A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot.

This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.
In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery , but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy.

Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.

In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label.
The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan , the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives , and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations.

Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.

Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation . This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.

Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money.

In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.

The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters . In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.

There is nothing comparable to these laws in Alaska, however, and whether laws like this could prevent this type of thing in a federal election is still untested. Under the Supreme Court’s decision in U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton in 1995, states cannot add their own qualifications for Congress.

The advice from 1860 – “Watch your tickets on election day. There’s a scheme on foot …” – when newspapers urged voters to read their tickets before casting their vote, is still relevant long after the demise of the party ticket. It is unlikely that the law can solve this problem, because to do so would be to wade into the First Amendment waters of why people run for office. Regulating thought and intention is a dangerous proposition under the Constitution.
The old answer is the best one. Self-government depends less on clever rules and more on citizens paying attention. Read your ballots!

Drew Kurlowski does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Allegheny County is reassessing every property – here’s how your tax bill is calculated now
articles.author:
<name>Elizabeth Jane Beckett-Camarata, Professor of Public Administration, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/elizabeth-jane-beckett-camarata-2764336"/>
paras: Allegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years .

The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down.

For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill.
In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services.
I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg , including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work.
The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes.

An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia , assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois , which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market.

Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969 .
Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal .

Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value.
Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate .

For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills.
Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts.

The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise.

School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools . They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs.

School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny , one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates .
Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills.

The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50 , cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption , which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once.

The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77 , takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369.

Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review . Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person.

Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin.

At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it.

Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment.

That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012.

articles.title: Why achieving your goals can leave you feeling so empty
articles.author:
<name>Stacy Keltner, Chair of the Department of Interdisciplinary Studies and Professor of Philosophy, Kennesaw State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/stacy-keltner-336357"/>
paras: When Anne Carson learned she had won the Nobel Prize in literature, she was in Iceland, where, according to the Swedish Academy , she was “listening to the wind.”
Carson didn’t answer her phone right away, silencing it until her husband persuaded her to call back . Her verdict on the academy’s choice: “I think you’re all insane.”
Whatever she felt in the moment, there is an irony in Carson’s Nobel win. The highest award in literature has gone to a writer who has spent her career exploring the emptiness of a desire fulfilled.
The honor coincides with the 40th anniversary of the publication of her first book, “ Eros the Bittersweet ,” a meditation on desire.

In it, Carson argues that desire begins with a void – with wanting what we don’t have. She traces how this feeling of absence shapes love, reading, writing and thinking, activities that renew themselves precisely because they are never complete.

“Eros” begins with a brief preface on Franz Kafka’s “ The Top ,” a story about a philosopher who spends his time around children so he can chase their spinning tops. When a child sets a top in motion, the philosopher snatches it, believing that understanding any small thing, even a spinning top, would be enough to understand everything.
While the top spins, the philosopher is filled with hope, but as soon as he grasps it, he is repelled by the dumb piece of wood. He throws it down and waits for the next child to spin a top.

For Carson, the story is about why people love to fall in love. The philosopher is after what Carson calls an “impertinent stability in vertigo,” a state that is “itself delightful, a suspended moment of living hope.” The philosopher’s quest for knowledge, Carson cheekily concludes, is simply his pretext for chasing spinning tops. He is enchanted by the spinning itself, and even by his own enchantment – a spell that breaks the instant the top stops in his hand.

Most people know a version of this: There is something animating about chasing a goal. But once attained, the framed degree fades into the wall, the promotion quickly loses its luster, and the plaque becomes another dumb piece of wood.
The delight of wanting disappears in the having.
Why does fulfillment so often feel like loss?

Carson’s answer begins with the Greek word for erotic love, “eros,” which she explains denotes want or lack. Plato’s Socrates makes the same point in the “ Symposium .” For the Greeks, no one desires what they already have.

Desire also opens up an absence. To long for someone or something is to discover our own edges, the chasm where the self ends and what is wanted begins. Eros reveals that we are incomplete – an awareness that causes the self to become undone, loosening at the joints.
In one of her poems, the Greek poet Sappho called this experience “ glukupikron ,” or “sweetbitter.”
Carson’s translation of the passage reads : “Eros once again limb-loosener whirls me / sweetbitter, impossible to fight off, creature stealing up.”

Sappho puts sweet first, Carson notes in “Eros,” but desire is not initially sweet and then bitter. Pleasure and pain arrive together, in the same body and at the same time, before the lover is even able to distinguish them.

Carson extends this pattern to reading, writing and thinking. A reader approaches a text’s meaning but never masters it; every rereading turns up new meanings. The pleasure of understanding and the ache of incompleteness arrive together.

Writing works the same way. A good sentence both captures and conceals what the writer means. Thinking also runs on that doubled feeling, which is how the story of a philosopher chasing tops ended up in a book about love.
The same bittersweet pattern also shows up somewhere far less romantic: at work. Meeting a deadline brings relief that is already hollow because the next one is waiting.

I discovered “Eros the Bittersweet” as a philosophy graduate student, when my goals were to read, write and think my way into questions I loved. Now I spend much of my day as a university administrator, where the quality of my work is measured in metrics and met deadlines. Somewhere along the way, my goals stopped being things I wanted and became things to check off.

Today’s productivity culture chases tops of its own, but it looks less like Kafka’s philosopher than like Lucy and Ethel working at the chocolate factory in the 1952 “ I Love Lucy ” episode “ Job Switching .” As the conveyor belt speeds up, the only way they can look like they’re keeping up is to stuff what they’ve missed into their mouths.

Few things capture this pressure more than the SMART goal. In 1981, management consultant George Doran proposed that goals be SMART : specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related. The acronym spread through industries and disciplines as a model for strategic planning, project management, performance evaluations and personal goal-setting. It distills a wider creed: Set the target, sprint after it, hit it. Grasp the top, toss it, capture the next one, ad infinitum. Doran didn’t invent the impulse, but his acronym gave it a checklist.
Carson’s account of desire helps explain why this creed leads to two kinds of emptiness.

The first comes from pursuing goals people never really desired. Inbox zero and a quarterly metric are goals in service of goals, the ultimate of which is productivity itself, which often simply ends up boosting someone else’s productivity.

The second comes from goals people truly wanted. Psychologist Tal Ben-Shahar calls the letdown that follows the “ arrival fallacy ” – the belief that reaching a destination will bring lasting happiness.

The Greeks offer another kind of striving, one that locates pleasure in the pursuit itself rather than in the prize. In Plato’s “ Phaedrus ,” Socrates describes eros as giving the soul wings and treats philosophy as a love of wisdom no one can own.

Centuries later, philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre distinguished external goods, such as money and status, from goods internal to a practice, such as a farmer’s growing mastery of her land or an architect’s pursuit of elegant, functional design. MacIntyre’s example, in his 1981 book “ After Virtue ,” is a child paid in candy to learn chess. As long as she plays for the candy, she has every reason to cheat. Only when she comes to love the game does she gain what chess itself can give: a particular kind of analytical skill, strategic imagination and competitive intensity.
To Socrates, MacIntyre and Carson, external goods get used up as they are won. Internal goods deepen the longer we pursue them.

Keeping desire alive means choosing pursuits that can never be finished – a craft, a field of study, a relationship – and letting the gap between reaching and grasping stay open. In this way, the lack that can hollow us out can also be what moves us.

Carson was handed the highest prize in literature. Yet the picture the Swedish Academy left us with is of a writer standing in the Icelandic wind, attending to a force of nature that no one can catch.

articles.title: Florida Department of Health considers dropping 4 school vaccine requirements – here’s what that could mean for kids
articles.author:
<name>Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katrine-l-wallace-2626740"/>
paras: The Florida Department of Health held a hearing in October 2026 on a proposal to remove four vaccine requirements for entry into school and childcare: Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib , chickenpox , pneumococcal and hepatitis B .

These vaccines entered use in the U.S. at different times from the early 1980s through 2000. Prior to that, there were millions of chickenpox cases and thousands of serious bacterial infections and preventable deaths among American children each year. Vaccination has dramatically reduced the toll of these diseases.

Many parents today grew up during the transition to widespread vaccination for these diseases and may never have witnessed the severe complications these vaccines help prevent. I’m an epidemiologist who studies vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication , and I worry that perhaps the luxury of forgetting about these diseases could end up giving rise to a generation of children who aren’t vaccinated against them.

School vaccination requirements help communities establish herd immunity , which is when enough people are vaccinated to prevent a disease from easily spreading. When vaccination rates fall, infections can spread among susceptible children throughout the community, placing those who are too young to be fully vaccinated, as well as those who cannot develop adequate protection due to medical conditions, at greater risk.

Florida’s proposal would not eliminate these four vaccines, nor would ending a mandate mean that every family would stop using them. However, it would weaken one of the policies designed to maintain high vaccination coverage. If fewer children are vaccinated as a result, the risks will extend beyond the families making that choice.

Before Hib vaccines became widely used in the late 1980s, pediatricians sometimes faced a terrifying emergency: an infant with fever, lethargy and a stiff neck. Testing of cerebrospinal fluid would reveal bacterial meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib , an infection that could kill a child or leave lasting neurological damage.
Today, many doctors have never even seen a single case. The bacterium has not disappeared, but widespread vaccination has made serious Hib disease in young children far less common.

Before the vaccine, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis . In the early 1980s, there were 20,000 invasive Hib infections among American children under 5 years old, 12,000 of which were meningitis. Between 3% and 6% of those children died , and between 15% and 30% of the survivors were left deaf or with brain damage.
Hib infection did not manifest in dramatic outbreaks. Healthy young children carried it silently, and some, unpredictably, became seriously ill.

After the introduction of conjugate vaccines for Hib in the late 1980s, cases among young children declined by 99% . In 2023, the United States reported only 13 cases in children under 5 . In 2026, that number is up to 28 .

By the early 1990s, there were more than 4 million cases of chickenpox annually in the United States. Of those infected, 10,500 to 13,500 were hospitalized, and 100 to 150 died. More than 90% of cases and about 70% of hospitalizations occurred in children, as did roughly half of the deaths.
But even those who had manageable cases of childhood chickenpox are at risk for shingles later in life, which can lead to painful and sometimes permanent health complications .

Children are contagious before the rash appears, and each case has an incubation period of up to three weeks . A single infection could spread through a school or daycare in waves for a month or more. Since vaccination began in 1995, deaths from chickenpox in people under 20 years old have been virtually eliminated .
Pneumococcal bacteria can live harmlessly in a child’s upper respiratory tract – that is, the nose – but if it moves into the blood or organs, it can cause serious damage.

Before the introduction of the childhood vaccine in 2000, pneumococcal disease caused about 17,000 invasive infections annually in American children under 5 years old, including about 700 cases of meningitis and 200 deaths . On top of that, pneumococcal disease caused approximately 5 million ear infections.

Hepatitis B can spread from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth and through contact with infected blood. People with chronic hepatitis B may have no symptoms and may not know they are infected, allowing the virus to spread unknowingly within families and communities. Infected infants and young children also are often asymptomatic.

Yet the consequences can be serious. Infants who become infected with hepatitis B have about a 90% chance of developing chronic hepatitis B , which over time can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The risk of chronic infection falls sharply with age, making prevention of infection early in life particularly important.
Before the hepatitis B vaccine became available in the U.S. in 1982, an estimated 20,000 American children were infected each year.

In 1991, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended universal infant hepatitis B vaccination as part of a comprehensive strategy to prevent transmission. The CDC estimates that perinatal hepatitis B infections in the United States declined by 75% between 1987 and 2000.

Florida’s historical records for these diseases are incomplete. For example, chickenpox was not a disease tracked by the Florida Department of Health until late 2006 . That makes it difficult to reconstruct the state’s prevaccine impact of these diseases from surveillance records alone.

But Florida doesn’t have to imagine what happens when vaccination is neglected: Measles has resurfaced in the state this year. It had previously been eliminated nationally in 2000 , meaning sustained endemic transmission had been interrupted. The disease has never been eradicated globally, and imported infections can trigger outbreaks when they reach undervaccinated communities.

An outbreak at Ave Maria University outside of Naples infected at least 62 people , and the state reported 162 cases as of Oct. 17, 2026. This is the most recent available data at the time of this article’s publication.

The proposal to stop requiring vaccines for hepatitis B, chickenpox, Hib and pneumococcal comes as only 88.9% of Florida kindergartners received the measles, mumps, rubella – or MMR – vaccine during the 2025-26 school year. This is below both the U.S. national average of 92.4% and the recommended threshold of 95% to create herd immunity.

Unfortunately, it’s been difficult to know current measles rates in Florida. In May 2026, the Florida Department of Health removed county-level disease data from its website. The data has since been replaced, but there is currently no measles dashboard to track cases in the state. The department’s 2026 counts have often been delayed , and public tracking systems disagree on the statewide total.

An entire generation of parents has been spared the experience of seeing a child with Hib meningitis, or young adults with liver problems from chronic hepatitis B. Nor have they had to deal with finding alternate childcare for a month because a chickenpox outbreak has shut down their child’s preschool. These are achievements of vaccination – and a reminder of what can be forgotten when prevention works.
